# Romans 2: Research Notes for a Verse-by-Verse Commentary

**What I couldn't find:** I found no pages from Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), Orthodox sites (oca.org), modern scholarship sites (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org), or on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching about Romans 2. Those are left out. Chrysostom, a Church Father honoured by both Orthodox and Catholics, appears for vv. 17–21 only, from Bible Hub. The Bible Hub page labelled as his comment on v. 5 actually covered Romans 3, so I didn't use it. Fetched pages have no line-level citations, so they are shown by URL only.

---

## Verses 1–5: The person who judges others

**v. 1**
- **Traditional:** By judging others, the moralist appeals to an outside standard, and that standard condemns him too. As we judge another person, we point to a standard outside of our self – and that standard condemns everyone, not only the obvious sinner. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-2/)
- **Link to 1:32:** Most commentators, therefore, hold that the inference therefore in Ro 2:1 is drawn from Ro 1:32, where it is said that all men know that those who sin are worthy of death. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_21-2)
- **Who is addressed:** Wesley says Paul now turns from the Gentiles to the Jews. Paul uses the general "O man" and does not yet call him a Jew. "Inexcusable" means knowing what is right without doing it only adds to guilt. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm) Bible.org agrees the target is the Jew who judges Gentiles: when he judges, he admits that such behavior is wrong, and worthy of just punishment from God, yet he himself knowingly commits the same sins. (https://bible.org/seriespage/study-and-exposition-romans-21-16)

**v. 2**
- "According to truth" most likely means God judges people according to the real nature of their conduct, and not as their conduct may appear to people. (Barnes, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/2-2.htm)
- Wesley says the judgment is fair, makes no exceptions, and reaches the heart as well as outward behaviour. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)

**v. 3**
- Matthew Henry imagines asking the sinner whether he really thinks the heart-searching God be imposed upon by formal pretences, the righteous Judge of all so bribed and put off? (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_002.cfm)
- Wesley reads "escape" as escape *rather than the Gentile*. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)

**v. 4**
- **Three words:** Guzik takes "goodness" as God's kindness about our *past* sin. "Forbearance" is His kindness about our *present* sin. He calls longsuffering kindness toward future sin. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-2/)
- **The danger:** Men misinterpret God's forbearance and longsuffering as His approval, and they refuse to repent. (same URL)
- **Wesley:** Despising God's kindness goes a step beyond hoping to escape His anger: it abuses His love. "Leads you" means God *intends* His kindness to encourage repentance. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)

**v. 5**
- **Storing up wrath:** JFB pictures the sinner piling up an ever accumulating stock of divine wrath, like a hoard of treasure. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rom/Rom_002.cfm)
- **Jewish background:** Precept Austin notes some Jewish traditions (see note above) speak of treasuring up good works against the day of wrath. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_25-8)
- **The day of wrath:** Guzik says God's love was shown most clearly at Jesus' first coming. At the second coming of Jesus the righteous judgment of God will be revealed most clearly. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-2/)
- **God's anger:** Matthew Henry says God's wrath is not a burst of passion. It is a righteous judgment, his will to punish sin, because he hates it as contrary to his nature. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_002.cfm)

---

## Verses 6–11: Judgment by deeds

**v. 6**
- **Traditional:** Alford, quoted by Precept Austin, says Paul is describing how God governs the world in general. No question at present arises, how this righteousness in God's sight is to be obtained. That question is answered later. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_25-8)
- Precept Austin sums up: Paul is not describing the basis for salvation but the basis for judgment. (same URL)

**vv. 6–7: Where traditions differ**
- **Hypothetical view:** Bible Hub's Q&A says Paul assumes, for the sake of argument, that a flawless doer of good would receive life. Then in 3:9 he shows no one actually is one. (https://biblehub.com/q/Is_Romans_2_7_about_works_or_faith.htm)
- **Reformed (monergism.com):** Romans 2:6–16 is "law, not gospel". The covenant of works really does demand perfect obedience, and only Christ has met it. The article says Catholic theology, the New Perspective on Paul, Federal Vision and "future justification" ideas go wrong by softening Romans 2. Judgment Day, then, is not a future justification based on our works. It is the public acknowledgment of a verdict already rendered. (https://www.monergism.com/reformation-theology/blog/romans-26%E2%80%9316-law-not-gospel-covenant-works-still-stands-only-christ-has)
- **Charismatic (Sam Storms):** Storms holds firmly to grace through faith. He argues the faith that saves is the "faith" that "obeys." Such faith gradually changes a person's life. (https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/-11-so-is-salvation-by-faith-or-by-works-romans-26-11)
- **Wesleyan:** Wesley's brief note on v. 7 says seeking glory is fine, because pure love does not exclude faith, hope, desire. *(Note: that citation number is wrong. The quoted words come from https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm, not the CCEL result.)*
- **Catholic (catholic.com):** Romans 2:6–7 is described as one of those passages used often by Catholics when talking to Protestants about the role works play in our salvation. (https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/works-mattered-to-st-paul) A follow-up article argues Paul means the *final* stage of salvation, not the first. It rejects the Protestant reading that works are only evidence of faith. It concludes good works, along with faith, play a crucial part in final salvation. (https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/works-mattered-to-st-paul-part-two) Another article says The works that justify us (as we saw in Romans 2:6-7) are works done *in Christ*. (https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/are-good-works-necessary-for-salvation)
- **Other evangelical view:** JFB says the final judgment will turn upon *character* alone. It links "patient continuance" to Luke 8:15, where it describes the lasting, growing nature of new life. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rom/Rom_002.cfm)

**v. 8**
- Wesley pictures the "contentious" as the Jew who fights against God. He says the words "indignation and wrath" echo Psalm 78:49 and the plagues of Egypt. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)
- Matthew Henry's Concise calls contention the principle of all evil. *(Note: that citation number is wrong. The quoted words come from https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/2-13.htm, Matthew Henry's Concise.)*

**v. 9**
- **"Jew first":** Since Jews come first for the gospel and first for reward, then they are also first in line for judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-2/)
- Wesley says their training in true religion places them in the foremost rank of the guilty. *(Note: that citation number is wrong. The quoted words come from https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm.)*

**v. 10**
- Wesley pairs each blessing with its opposite in v. 9. Glory is the opposite of wrath, honour the opposite of indignation, and peace, "now and for ever", the opposite of trouble and distress. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)

**v. 11**
- Wesley says God's fairness fits with His freely giving people different advantages and opportunities as He chooses. (same URL)
- Matthew Henry: fair justice means giving frowns and favours with respect to deserts and without respect to persons. (https://ccel.org/study/Rom_2?comm=2)

---

## Verses 12–16: Law, conscience and judgment

**v. 12**
- Wesley says those "without law" are condemned by the law written in their hearts. Paul writes "perish" rather than "be judged" because there is no outward law to judge them by. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)
- Bible.org frames 12–16 as being not about salvation, but about the method of God's righteous judgment: Jews by the law of Moses, Gentiles by their conscience. (https://bible.org/seriespage/study-and-exposition-romans-21-16)

**v. 13: A key verse where traditions differ**
- **Hypothetical reading (the majority):** Barnes says this is a general principle of law. Perfect, lifelong obedience would justify, but it doesn't claim anyone has done it. Poole says no one, "natural nor regenerate," can keep the law like this, so justification must come another way. The Geneva notes agree. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/2-13.htm) John Stott is quoted as calling it a theoretical or hypothetical statement. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/there-is-no-partiality-with-god-part-2)
- **Gill's two options:** Read it as hypothetical, or as believers counted as perfect law-keepers *in Christ*, their substitute. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/romans/2-13.html)
- **Baptist (John Piper):** Piper says Paul means there really are such people, and they are the only ones acquitted at the judgment. When Christ comes into a person's life by the power of the Holy Spirit through faith in the Gospel, that person becomes a "doer of the law." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/there-is-no-partiality-with-god-part-2) He adds that the verse states no cause: It does not say "by doing the works of the law you will be justified." So it doesn't contradict 3:20. (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/how-our-faith-and-law-keeping-work-together-in-the-christian-life)
- **Bible.org:** Takes a similar line. Paul is describing a *direction* of obedience that Spirit-born people actually practise, not earned justification. (https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-11-god-s-impartial-judgment-romans-212-16)
- **Wesleyan:** Wesley says the doers of the law will be "finally acquitted and rewarded". (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm) The Benson Commentary, which uses Wesley's wording, goes further. Paul does not mean flawless obedience, it says, but a sincere "obedience of faith". By grace and for Christ's sake, God accepts it in place of perfect righteousness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/2-13.htm)
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Quotes Calvin: "If righteousness be sought from the law, the law must be fulfilled; for the righteousness of the law consists in the perfection of works." Paul's point is to knock down the idea that being born Jewish makes you safe at the judgment. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/work-law-heart)
- **Ellicott:** Hearing the law gives no exemption from judgment. Only keeping it would, and that could apply to Gentiles as much as to Jews. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/2-13.htm)

**v. 14: Which Gentiles?**
- **Majority view (unsaved pagans):** Bible.org says Paul means not to Gentiles who are Christians, but rather to Gentiles as people without the Mosaic law (and by implication unsaved). (https://bible.org/seriespage/study-and-exposition-romans-21-16)
- **Alternative view (Gentile Christians):** Bible.org notes others hear an echo of Jeremiah 31:33 and think the Gentiles Paul has in mind here are Christians. (same URL)
- **Ligonier:** Even pagans know enough of our Creator's requirements to do what He requires. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/work-law-heart)
- **Wesleyan:** Wesley adds that "by nature" really means by *preventing grace*, God's grace at work before conversion. He calls the Ten Commandments the "substance of the law of nature". (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)
- **Catholic:** Catholic.com reads this as the natural moral law, a moral law inscribed within the very fabric of our human nature that is accessible to reason alone. (https://www.catholic.com/bible-navigator/contraception/romans214-15)
- **Pagan parallels:** Precept Austin cites Sophocles and Plutarch on an "unwritten law" and says Paul borrows that idea. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_213-16)

**v. 15**
- **Wording:** Leon Morris, quoted by Guzik, points out Paul does not say the law itself is written on their hearts, but the *work of the law*, what the law requires of people. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-2/)
- **Guzik:** Conscience is enough to condemn, and in theory enough to justify. (same URL)
- **Wesley:** Uses a courtroom picture. Conscience and sin are witnesses, and the person's thoughts argue like plaintiff and defendant. The wording suggests there is "far more room to accuse than to defend". (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)
- **Gill:** The law was written perfectly on Adam's heart, was spoiled by the fall, and is written again on the heart at regeneration. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/niv/romans/2-15.html)
- **When does the accusing happen?** Bible.org argues it happens *now*, not only at the final judgment. (https://bible.org/seriespage/study-and-exposition-romans-21-16)

**v. 16**
- JFB says "secrets" refers especially to the unfathomed depths of hypocrisy in the self-righteous. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rom/Rom_002.cfm)
- Wesley says the real quality of actions depends on hidden circumstances, often unknown even to the person. He concludes from "my gospel" that the gospel "also is a law". (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)
- Matthew Henry's Concise: nothing is more frightening to sinners, or more comforting to saints, than Christ being the Judge. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/2-13.htm)

---

## Verses 17–24: The Jew who relies on the law

**vv. 17–18**
- **Chrysostom:** Paul says "you *call yourself*" a Jew, not "you are" one. He says "you *know*" God's will, not "you do" it. Chrysostom sees Paul gently mocking their pride. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/romans/2.htm)
- **Wesley:** Lays out ten points of boasting: five about themselves (vv. 17–18) and five about others (vv. 19–20). Relying on the law means depending on something that can only condemn. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)

**vv. 19–20**
- Wesley says "blind," "in darkness," "foolish" and "infants" were names Jews commonly gave Gentiles. (same URL)
- Chrysostom notes Paul writes "you are *convinced*", meaning "so you boast". He says they had knowledge "in the law", not in conscience or good deeds. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/romans/2.htm)

**vv. 21–22**
- **Chrysostom:** Paul puts it as a question, which is gentler than in vv. 1–3. He applies it to Christians: hypocritical believers lose their witness to unbelievers. Greed and other passions are a kind of idolatry. (same URL)
- **"Rob temples":** A footnote on that page gives three readings: robbing pagan temples (Chrysostom's view), robbing the Jerusalem temple, or "sacrilege" in general (Calvin, Luther, Bengel). (same URL)
- **Wesley:** Takes it as sacrilege, robbing God of His glory. He cites Jewish priests of the time who lived by robbery, and Malachi's complaint about robbing God. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)

**vv. 23–24**
- Wesley gives the source of the quotation as Isaiah 52:5. (same URL)
- Bible Hub's overview names "Hypocrisy destroys witness" as a key theme. (https://biblehub.com/romans/2.htm)

---

## Verses 25–29: True circumcision

**v. 25**
- Wesley notes Paul says circumcision "profits", not that it "justifies". He adds: The very same observation holds with regard to baptism. *(Note: that citation number is wrong. The quoted sentence comes from https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm.)*

**vv. 26–27**
- **Guzik:** Asks whether a Gentile keeping the law through conscience would be justified instead of a law-breaking Jew. His point: *having* the law or *having* a ceremony isn't enough. God requires *righteousness*. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-2/)
- **Piper (Baptist):** Reads these verses as describing real Gentile believers who become "true Jews". Fulfilling the law means experiencing this heart change by the Spirit, and then living in sync with that inner change. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/who-is-a-true-jew-part-2)
- **Wesley:** "Keeping the law" here means keeping its substance. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)

**v. 28**
- **Matthew Henry:** This is not meant to drive us away from outward ordinances, but from trusting to them and resting in them as sufficient to bring us to heaven. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/2-28.html)

**v. 29: Is "spirit" the Holy Spirit or the human spirit?**
- **Barnes:** It does not mean by the Holy Spirit, but that the work was to take place in the soul, and not in the body only. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/2-29.htm)
- **Gill:** Allows either the human soul or God's Spirit. (same URL)
- **Wesley:** Combines the two: the inmost soul, renewed by the Spirit of God. He links it to Deuteronomy 30:6. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/2.htm)
- **Precept Austin:** Firmly the Holy Spirit, supernatural surgery by the Holy Spirit. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_227-29)
- **Piper:** Ties it to three works of the Spirit: circumcising the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6), writing the law on it (Jeremiah 31:33), and freeing us from needing people's praise. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/who-is-a-true-jew-part-2)
- **Coffman:** Paul isn't saying the outward rite was unnecessary under the law. He means the rite *alone*, without a godly life, was worthless. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/2-29.html)
- **Application:** Bible Hub's commentary page prays that we be baptized, not with water only, but with the Holy Ghost. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/2-29.htm)
- **"Praise from God":** Guzik says outward signs of religion may win praise from people, but never from God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-2/)
